metrics.name: structure
metrics.feedback: Complexity and function length are within limits.

metrics.name: complexity
metrics.feedback: Consistent with O(1): all runs finished below the 30 ms timing noise floor (max 1.5 ms), so growth could not be measured - use larger sizes for a firm verdict.

metrics.name: readability
metrics.feedback: LLM unavailable - heuristic readability only (comments 14%, avg name length 4.0).

usefulness.example: A 300-student C programming lab collects add.c files. The agent compiles, sandboxes and scores each file under the same rules in a few seconds per submission, and writes one JSON + text report per student.
usefulness.benefit: Every student is graded by identical, reproducible rules, and TAs spend their time on borderline cases instead of running 300 programs by hand.

usefulness.use_case: Instant self-check feedback before the deadline
usefulness.example: A student submits int a,b; printf("%d", a+b) and immediately sees the failing input 2147483647 1 with the expected output 2147483648 and an explanation of signed overflow.
usefulness.benefit: Students learn from a concrete counter-example while they can still fix the program, not weeks later from a mark.

usefulness.example: Two submissions that differ only in variable names and comments reach a token-similarity of 1.00 against the 0.85 threshold and are flagged. The instructor reviews that pair instead of reading all 300 files.
usefulness.benefit: Narrows manual integrity checking to the few suspicious pairs.

usefulness.example: A company runs 500 candidate submissions for an 'add two integers safely' task. The agent ranks them by correctness, edge-case handling and memory safety and gives a per-metric explanation.
usefulness.benefit: Fast first-round filtering where every rejection can be justified metric by metric.

limitations.example: A program that hard-codes the answers for the 10 visible inputs (if (a==7 && b==5) puts("12");) or only handles the whitespace layouts used in the tests still scores 10/10 on correctness, and also passes the built-in edge cases it happens to special-case.
limitations.mitigation: Differential testing against the reference solution on extra edge cases and LLM-proposed counter-tests; keep a hidden test set larger than the published one.

limitations.limitation: Empirical complexity estimation is noisy and size-limited
limitations.example: With sizes [1, 10, 100] an O(n^2) solution runs in under 1 ms, so every run is below the timing noise floor and the agent reports 'consistent with the required bound' instead of detecting the quadratic growth. Likewise an O(n) program with a huge constant can be mislabelled O(1).
limitations.mitigation: Use large sizes and an input generator in the rules (e.g. n up to 10^5); treat 'inconclusive' verdicts as 'needs human review'.

limitations.limitation: Similarity and AI-copy detection give false positives and false negatives
limitations.example: For a trivial task two honest students both write the same 8-line program and have similarity 1.00 (the min_tokens guard silences very short files, which then become uncheckable). Conversely, code copied from the web is only caught if that solution is already in the corpus folders, and a restructured ChatGPT answer produces low similarity and escapes.
limitations.mitigation: Flags are triage only: a human must review them; keep adding known online/LLM solutions to reference_corpus/.

limitations.limitation: LLM readability scores are subjective and model-dependent
limitations.example: A small 8B local model rates a file full of useless comments such as '// add a and b' higher than clean, idiomatic C with no comments. Switching the model in the rules (llama3.1 to qwen2.5-coder) can move the readability score by 2-3 points. Identical results rely on the on-disk response cache.
limitations.mitigation: Fixed rubric prompt, temperature 0, seed 42, response cache, and a 30% heuristic blend; re-grade with the same model and cache for official marks.
